claims.text: An MTP+FEP workflow for TaVCrW will reduce computational cost by more than 80% relative to TOR-TILD.
The MTP+FEP workflow will maintain sub-meV accuracy for TaVCrW thermodynamic properties.
Equimolar TaVCrW is a disordered BCC solid solution at 0 K.
Short-range order stabilizes TaVCrW by approximately 2–3 meV/atom.
Training an MTP on solid, liquid, and high-temperature TaVCrW configurations can cover the relevant phase space.
FEP using an MTP can replace the TI pathway for estimating the free-energy difference between the TaVCrW solid and liquid.
A supercell containing more than 500 atoms is required to avoid finite-size effects on TaVCrW SRO and liquid structure.
The relevant validation temperature range is 2000–2400 K.
The MTP must reproduce the ab initio phase-space distributions of both solid and liquid TaVCrW, including SRO and relevant electronic-structure variations.
Accurate reproduction of the ab initio phase-space distribution enables rapid convergence of the FEP estimator.
Prior same-system work demonstrates that MTP-aided thermodynamic integration can simulate high-temperature TaVCrW properties with less than 1 meV/atom error and a fourfold speedup.
FEP can sample configurations from a solid reference state and perturb directly to a liquid target state, thereby avoiding TI's sequential sampling.
Capturing the 2–3 meV/atom SRO stabilization and electronic density-of-states gap effects is necessary to preserve melting-point accuracy.
MTP evaluation scales as O(N) or O(N log N), whereas DFT scales as O(N^3).
FEP will converge faster than TI for TaVCrW.
The MTP+FEP result will differ from a high-fidelity DFT-TI baseline by less than 0.5 meV/atom.
The predicted TaVCrW melting temperature will be within 20–30 K of the DFT-TILD value.
Neglecting high-temperature magnetic fluctuations in V and Cr can shift the melting point by tens of kelvin.
The usual GGA-PBE/LDA underbinding and overbinding rules fail for V and Cr at 0 K and may propagate errors into the workflow.
FEP accuracy depends strongly on phase-space overlap between the sampled reference and target distributions.
